source_text: Insuper argumentandi libidine ex forma ingenii haeretici locum sibi fecit Alexander ille, quasi nos affirmemus idcirco Christum terreni census induisse carnem, ut evacuaret in semetipso carnem peccati. Quod etsi diceremus, quacunque ratione muniremus sententiam nostram, dum ne tanta amentia, qua putavit tanquam ipsam carnem Christi opinemur ut peccatricem evacuatam in ipso, cum illam et ad dexteram patris in caelis praesidere meminerimus, et venturam inde suggestu paternae claritatis praedicemus, adeo ut evacuatam non possumus dicere, ita nec peccatricem nec evacuatam in qua dolus non fuit. Defendimus autem non carnem peccati evacuatam esse in Christo, sed peccatum carnis, non materiam, sed naturam, nec substantiam, sed culpam, secundum apostoli auctoritatem, dicentis, Evacuavit peccatum in carne. Nam et alibi, In similitudine, inquit, carnis peccati fuisse Christum, non quod similitudinem carnis acceperit, quasi imaginem corporis et non veritatem, sed similitudinem peccatricis carnis vult intellegi; quod ipsa non peccatrix caro Christi eius fuit par cuius erat peccatum, genere, non vitio Adae: quando hinc etiam confirmamus eam fuisse carnem in Christo cuius natura est in homine peccatrix, et sic in illa peccatum evacuatum, quod in Christo sine peccate habeatur quae in homine sine peccato non habebatur. Nam neque ad propositum Christi faceret, evacuantis peccatum carnis, non in ea carne evacuare illud in qua erat natura peccati, neque ad gloriam. Quid enim magnum, si in carne meliore et alterius, id est non peccatricis naturae, naevum peccati redemit? Ergo, inquis, si nostram induit, peccatrix fuit caro Christi. Noli constringere explicabilem sensum. Nostram enim induens suam fecit; suam faciens non peccatricem eam fecit. Ceterum quod ad omnes dictum sit qui ideo non putant carnem nostram in Christo fuisse quia non fuit ex viri semine, recordentur Adam ipsum in hanc carnem non ex semine viri factum. Sicut terra conversa est in hanc carnem sine viri semine, ita et dei verbum potuit sine coagulo in eiusdem carnis transire materiam.
thought_title: Alexander's charge that Tertullian says Christ emptied sinful flesh
orientation: Tertullian is answering Alexander, who misrepresents him as saying Christ took earthly flesh in order to empty sinful flesh in himself.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, out of a love of arguing, from the pattern of a heretic's mind, that Alexander made a place for himself, as if we affirm that for this reason Christ put on flesh of earthly estate, so that he might empty in himself the flesh of sin. Even if we were to say this, by whatever reasoning we would fortify our opinion, provided that not with so great madness, by which he thought that we suppose the very flesh of Christ to be sinful, emptied in him, since we remember both that it presides at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, and we preach that it will come from there at the summons of the Father's glory, so that just as we cannot say it was emptied, so neither sinful nor emptied, the flesh in which there was no deceit. But we defend that not the flesh of sin was emptied in Christ, but the sin of the flesh, not the material, but the nature, not the substance, but the fault, according to the authority of the apostle, who says, He emptied sin in the flesh. For also elsewhere, In the likeness, he says, of flesh of sin Christ was, not that he received a likeness of flesh, as if an image of a body and not the truth, but he wants the likeness of sinful flesh to be understood; because the very non-sinful flesh of Christ was equal to that whose sin it was, in kind, not in the fault of Adam: whence from this also we confirm that the flesh in Christ was that whose nature in man is sinful, and so in it sin was emptied, because what in man was not had without sin is had in Christ without sin. For neither would it serve the purpose of Christ, who empties the sin of the flesh, to empty it not in that flesh in which was the nature of sin, nor would it serve his glory. For what great thing, if in a better flesh and of another, that is of a non-sinful nature, he redeemed the blemish of sin? Therefore, you say, if he put on ours, the flesh of Christ was sinful. Do not constrain a meaning that can be unfolded. For by putting on ours he made it his own; by making it his own he did not make it sinful. Moreover, what should be said to all who for this reason do not think our flesh was in Christ because it was not from the seed of a man, let them remember that Adam himself was made into this flesh not from the seed of a man. Just as earth was turned into this flesh without the seed of a man, so also the Word of God was able without coagulation to pass over into the material of the same flesh.

choices.why: census means condition or estate, not tax; 'earthly estate' keeps the legal/status sense of census while avoiding the false 'tax' reading
the verb evacuo is Tertullian's technical term for destroying or nullifying sin; 'empty' preserves the literal force and the repeated wordplay with evacuatam

choices.why: suggestus here means a prompting or summons; 'summons' keeps the active sense of the Father's glory calling Christ to return

choices.why: Tertullian is making a precise distinction between the physical stuff (materia, substantia) and the moral quality (natura, culpa); the literal pairings preserve the antithesis

choices.why: coagulum is a concrete term for curdling or thickening; 'coagulation' keeps the physical metaphor of how the Word could take flesh without human seed

choices.english: a meaning that can be unfolded
choices.why: explicabilis means capable of being unfolded or explained; the literal rendering preserves Tertullian's image of unfolding a compressed thought

pass_b_english: Moreover, that Alexander, out of his heretical cast of mind and love of argument, made room for himself by claiming that we assert Christ put on flesh of earthly estate precisely in order to empty in himself the flesh of sin. Even if we did say this, we would defend our position by whatever reasoning we could—so long as it is not that madness by which he supposed that we regard the very flesh of Christ as sinful and emptied in him, when we remember that it sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven, and we proclaim that it will come from there on the tribunal of the Father's glory. So far are we from being able to call it emptied, that we also cannot call it sinful or emptied, since in it there was no deceit.

But we defend not that the flesh of sin was emptied in Christ, but the sin of the flesh—not the material, but the nature, not the substance, but the fault—according to the authority of the apostle, who says, "He emptied sin in the flesh" (Romans 8:3). For elsewhere he says that Christ was "in the likeness of the flesh of sin" (Romans 8:3), not meaning that he took the likeness of flesh as if it were the image of a body and not the reality, but he wants us to understand the likeness of sinful flesh. For Christ's flesh itself was not sinful, but it was equal to that flesh whose sin was in it—equal in kind, not in the fault of Adam. From this we also confirm that the flesh in Christ was that whose nature is sinful in man, and that in it sin was emptied, because in Christ it is possessed without sin, whereas in man it was not possessed without sin.

For it would not serve Christ's purpose—he who empties the sin of the flesh—not to empty it in that flesh in which the nature of sin existed, nor would it serve his glory. For what great thing is it if he redeemed the blemish of sin in a better flesh of another, that is, of a non-sinful nature? "Therefore," you say, "if he put on our flesh, Christ's flesh was sinful." Do not compress a meaning that can be unfolded. For by putting on our flesh he made it his own; by making it his own he made it free of sin.

As for what should be said to all who think our flesh was not in Christ because it was not from the seed of a man, let them remember that Adam himself was made into this flesh not from the seed of a man. Just as the earth was turned into this flesh without the seed of a man, so also the Word was able to pass into the material of the same flesh without coagulation.

problems.fix: on the tribunal of the Father's glory.
problems.ruling: Suggestus means a raised platform or throne. 'At the summons of the Father's glory' replaces the place the flesh comes from with a call.

problems.source_quote: suam faciens non peccatricem eam fecit
problems.why: Non modifies peccatricem: he made the flesh non-sinful. The English only denies that he made it sinful.
problems.fix: by making it his own he made it free of sin.
problems.ruling: 'non peccatricem eam fecit' means he made it non-sinful, which is the point of the argument. 'Did not make it sinful' loses this.

last_rejected.fix: not its matter but its nature, not its substance but its fault
last_rejected.ruling: English matches Latin contrasts: non materiam→nature, non substantiam→fault

last_rejected.quote: equal in kind, not in the fault of Adam

last_rejected.fix: equal in kind, not by the fault of Adam
last_rejected.ruling: English conveys 'non vitio Adae' as not due to Adam's fault, same sense

last_rejected.why: The Latin says 'so we cannot call it emptied, nor sinful, nor emptied in which there was no deceit.' English adds 'So far are we...' and drops the logical connection 'ita nec peccatricem.'
last_rejected.fix: so that we cannot call it emptied, nor can we call it sinful or emptied, in which there was no deceit.

last_rejected.why: Coagulum is the coagulant (male seed as rennet), not the process of clotting. The clause says the Word entered the same flesh without that agent.
last_rejected.fix: so also the Word was able, without any coagulant, to pass into the material of the same flesh.
last_rejected.ruling: "sine coagulo" without coagulation is within range; coagulum can mean curdling/clotting, and Tertullian's point (no seed-induced coagulation) is preserved. Preference, not meaning change.
